## Introduction

I started this project because traffic accidents and congestion are
such a visible, everyday problem in Vietnam's cities, and I wanted to
try applying what I've learned about classification and imbalanced
data to a real road-safety question. The obvious first step — finding
a Vietnamese accident dataset — turned out to be a dead end: I checked,
and Hanoi's accident records are paper-based police forms, not open
data anywhere I could find.

So instead I picked a real, well-documented dataset chosen for its
**contextual** similarity rather than its origin: accident records from
Addis Ababa sub-city police (2017-2020). It's a developing-country,
mixed-vehicle urban traffic environment — motorcycles, pedestrians,
buses, and private cars sharing the same roads, with less-regulated
driving conditions — which felt a lot closer to Vietnam's own traffic
reality than the larger, better-known Western datasets I also
considered (US-Accidents, UK STATS19), which are purely car-centric
highway/suburban data. I want to be clear about what this claim is and
isn't: I'm not saying Ethiopian and Vietnamese traffic are the same,
only that the *kind* of problem — mixed-vehicle, developing urban road
network — is far more comparable than a US freeway dataset would be.

My task: predict accident **severity** from conditions known *before*
or *at* the moment of a crash — never from what happened to the people
involved afterward. The raw data records severity as 3 classes (Slight
/ Serious / Fatal injury), but as I'll show below, I ended up
deliberately collapsing that to a binary **Severe vs. Not Severe**
target instead, after measuring — not assuming — that the 3-class
version couldn't reliably detect the outcome that matters most.

## Data

12,316 real accident records, 32 raw columns.

```{python}
from traffic_accident_severity import config, data

df = data.load_accidents()
print(f"{len(df)} rows, {df.shape[1]} columns")
df[config.TARGET_COL].value_counts(normalize=True)
```

### The central data-understanding decision: excluding casualty outcomes

Looking through the raw columns, I noticed they split into two
fundamentally different kinds:

- **Pre-accident risk factors** (driver, vehicle, road, weather, time,
  collision dynamics) — knowable before/at the crash, the only kind of
  feature a real prevention or policy system could act on.
- **Post-accident casualty-outcome columns** (`Casualty_class`,
  `Casualty_severity`, `Sex_of_casualty`, `Age_band_of_casualty`,
  `Work_of_casuality`, `Fitness_of_casuality`, `Number_of_casualties`) —
  recorded *after* the crash, describing who got hurt and how.

This second group is a data-leakage trap I nearly walked into: using
these as features would be circular, since a system that needs to
already know how badly someone was hurt to predict how badly someone
was hurt isn't useful for anything. I excluded all of them up front.

```{python}
X, y = data.split_features_target(df)
print("Feature columns:", len(config.RAW_FEATURE_COLS))
print("Excluded casualty-outcome columns:", config.CASUALTY_OUTCOME_COLS)
```

### Real data-quality issues, found by checking rather than assuming

- **Severe missingness**: `Defect_of_vehicle` (~36%), `Service_year_of_vehicle`
  (~32%), `Work_of_casuality` (~26%), `Fitness_of_casuality` (~21%) —
  I used most-frequent imputation rather than dropping rows, which would
  have thrown away a large share of an already-small dataset.
- **Inconsistent time formatting**: I found that `Time` isn't always
  zero-padded — some rows are `"1:15:00"`, not `"01:15:00"`. My first
  attempt at parsing this with a naive string-slice silently corrupted
  single-digit hours; I only caught it while building this project's
  Streamlit app and noticing the hour distribution looked wrong.
  `pd.to_datetime(..., format="%H:%M:%S")` parses both forms correctly.

## Feature engineering

```{python}
from traffic_accident_severity.features import FeatureEngineer

engineered = FeatureEngineer().fit_transform(X)
engineered[["hour", "hour_sin", "hour_cos"]].describe().T
```

- **Circular hour-of-day encoding** (`hour_sin`/`hour_cos`) — hour 23
  and hour 0 are one hour apart, not "far away" from each other, so I
  placed hour on a 24-hour circle instead of leaving it as a plain
  integer — a standard technique for any periodic feature.
- **`RareCategoryGrouper`** on `Cause_of_accident` (20 distinct values),
  `Type_of_vehicle` (17), and `Area_accident_occured` (14) — a standard
  technique for long-tailed categorical variables generally.

## Choosing the modeling target: binary Severe, not raw 3-class

The raw target has 3 classes, and Fatal injury — the one that matters
most — is only ~1.3% of rows (~158 total). Before committing to
predicting all 3 classes, I wanted to measure whether that's actually
learnable, rather than assume it is just because the column exists.

```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
from traffic_accident_severity import model, config

X_raw = df[config.RAW_FEATURE_COLS]
y_raw = df[config.TARGET_COL]  # still the raw 3-class column here

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X_raw, y_raw, test_size=0.2, stratify=y_raw, random_state=config.RANDOM_SEED
)
raw_pipeline = model.build_pipeline(model.balanced_random_forest_estimator())
raw_pipeline.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(classification_report(y_test, raw_pipeline.predict(X_test), digits=3))
```

Even with class-weighting, Fatal injury's recall is around 3% — the
model is essentially not detecting it. There just aren't enough Fatal
rows for a model to reliably tell it apart from *two* other classes at
once. Rather than accept that, I tried collapsing Serious + Fatal into
one **Severe** class, which roughly doubles how much data the model has
to learn the pattern that matters (15.4% of rows vs. 1.3%):

```{python}
X, y = data.split_features_target(df)  # y is now binary: "Severe" vs "Not Severe"
print(y.value_counts(normalize=True))

X_train_b, X_test_b, y_train_b, y_test_b = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=config.RANDOM_SEED
)
severe_pipeline = model.build_pipeline(model.balanced_random_forest_estimator())
severe_pipeline.fit(X_train_b, y_train_b)
print(classification_report(y_test_b, severe_pipeline.predict(X_test_b), digits=3))
```

Recall for the outcome that matters most goes from ~3% to roughly
30-35% — a real, substantial improvement, not a marginal one. I decided
to make this the project's actual target from here on: every section
below (`X`, `y`) uses this binary Severe/Not-Severe framing, produced by
`data.split_features_target`, not the raw 3-class column. I think this
is also a more honest question for a real prevention system to answer
anyway — "is this likely to be a serious or fatal accident" is closer
to an actionable signal than "is this specifically fatal, as opposed to
merely serious."

## Methodology

### Why macro-F1, made concrete

```{python}
baseline = model.cross_validate_pipeline(X, y, estimator=model.random_forest_estimator(), cv=5)
print(f"Accuracy: {baseline['accuracy_mean']:.4f}")
print(f"Macro-F1: {baseline['f1_macro_mean']:.4f}")
```

The first time I ran this, the ~84.6% accuracy looked encouraging —
until I noticed it's almost exactly the majority-class ("Not Severe")
share. A model that mostly just predicts "Not Severe" for everything
would score similarly, which told me accuracy wasn't measuring what I
actually cared about. Macro-F1 told a very different story, exposing
how poorly that same model handles the Severe class. I used macro-F1
for every comparison from this point on.

### Class-imbalance handling, compared honestly

Severe is only ~15.4% of rows (~1,901 total) — still imbalanced enough
that it shapes every modeling decision from here on. I compared two
different fixes rather than assuming either one would help:

```{python}
imbalance_results = pd.DataFrame([
    {"approach": "Plain Random Forest", **model.cross_validate_pipeline(X, y, estimator=model.random_forest_estimator(), cv=5)},
    {"approach": "Random Forest + ADASYN", **model.cross_validate_pipeline(X, y, estimator=model.random_forest_estimator(), cv=5, resample=True)},
    {"approach": "Random Forest (class_weight=balanced)", **model.cross_validate_pipeline(X, y, estimator=model.balanced_random_forest_estimator(), cv=5)},
])
imbalance_results[["approach", "f1_macro_mean", "accuracy_mean"]]
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ax.barh(imbalance_results["approach"], imbalance_results["f1_macro_mean"], color=[PALETTE[3], PALETTE[2], PALETTE[0]])
ax.set_xlabel("Macro-F1")
plt.show()
```

**Class-weighting won clearly.** I don't think that's a rule to assume
for every imbalanced dataset — the better fix genuinely depends on the
data — which is exactly why I measured it directly instead of picking
one on instinct. With Severe at ~15.4% of rows, ADASYN's default
`n_neighbors=5` runs fine here — this needed lowering to 3 back when
the target was still the raw 3-class column and Fatal injury alone was
only ~1.3% of rows.

### Model comparison

```{python}
sweep_results = []
for name, factory in model.MODEL_FACTORIES.items():
    scores = model.cross_validate_pipeline(X, y, estimator=factory(), cv=5)
    sweep_results.append({"model": name, **scores})
sweep_df = pd.DataFrame(sweep_results).sort_values("f1_macro_mean", ascending=False)
sweep_df[["model", "f1_macro_mean", "accuracy_mean"]]
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.barh(sweep_df["model"], sweep_df["f1_macro_mean"], color=PALETTE[0])
ax.set_xlabel("Macro-F1")
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
plt.show()
```

`Random Forest (balanced)` beats even LightGBM and XGBoost here, which
surprised me a little going in — correctly handling the imbalance
mattered more than model sophistication.

## Choosing a decision threshold

`Random Forest (balanced)` outputs a *probability* of Severe, and
`.predict()` just applies a 0.5 cutoff to it internally. That cutoff
isn't special — since I get to choose it, the more useful question is
what precision/recall tradeoff is actually available at other cutoffs,
using out-of-fold predictions so I'm not fooling myself with predictions
the model already saw during training.

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score

severe_proba = model.cross_val_severe_probabilities(X, y, cv=5)
severe_preds_default = (severe_proba >= 0.5).astype(int)
y_numeric = (y == "Severe").astype(int)
print(classification_report(y_numeric, severe_preds_default, target_names=["Not Severe", "Severe"], digits=3))
```

At the default threshold, precision and recall for Severe are both
around 30% — not high in absolute terms, but a genuinely useful signal
compared to the ~3% Fatal recall the raw 3-class target gave. Since the
threshold is a free choice, the next step sweeps it directly.

```{python}
pr_auc = average_precision_score(y_numeric, severe_proba)
print(f"Average precision (PR-AUC): {pr_auc:.4f}  (base rate: {y_numeric.mean():.4f})")

threshold_sweep = model.severity_threshold_sweep(y, severe_proba, target_recalls=[0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9])
threshold_sweep
```

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.plot(threshold_sweep["recall"], threshold_sweep["precision"], marker="o", color=PALETTE[0])
for _, row in threshold_sweep.iterrows():
    ax.annotate(f"thr={row['threshold']:.2f}", (row["recall"], row["precision"]), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(6, 4))
ax.axhline(y_numeric.mean(), linestyle="--", color="gray", label="base rate")
ax.set_xlabel("Recall (share of Severe accidents caught)")
ax.set_ylabel("Precision (share of Severe alerts that are real)")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

The PR-AUC (~0.29) is roughly 2x the base rate (~0.154) — a real
improvement over guessing. The curve makes the tradeoff at the extremes
visible: to catch 90% of Severe accidents, precision drops to ~18% —
about 1 in 6 "Severe" alerts would be real. At the more conservative
30% recall end, precision is closer to 31%. Which threshold to actually
use is a policy decision, not a modeling one: it depends on how
expensive a false alarm is versus a missed Severe case, and that
tradeoff belongs to whoever would deploy this, not to the model. For a
*screening* tool — flagging conditions for a human road-safety reviewer
to look at more closely, not an automated response — I'd lean toward
the higher-recall end of this curve, since the cost of reviewing an
extra false alarm is much lower than missing a genuinely severe
pattern.

## Model interpretability

```{python}
from traffic_accident_severity.interpretability import compute_shap_values, top_shap_features

final_pipeline = model.train_pipeline(X, y, estimator=model.balanced_random_forest_estimator())
explanation, _ = compute_shap_values(final_pipeline, X, max_samples=500)
top = top_shap_features(explanation, top_n=12, class_index=1).sort_values("mean_abs_shap")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
ax.barh(top["feature"], top["mean_abs_shap"], color=PALETTE[0])
ax.set_xlabel("Mean |SHAP value| for the Severe class")
ax.set_title("Top 12 features driving Severe predictions")
plt.show()
```

### What these features would mean for Vietnam

The features SHAP ranks highest for Severe are almost all things a city
traffic authority can actually act on, which is what makes this more
than an academic exercise:

- **Number of vehicles involved** and **junction type** dominate —
  multi-vehicle collisions and crossing-type junctions carry
  disproportionate Severe risk. That points at *where* to intervene,
  not just *who* to blame.
- **Time of day** and **weather** show up clearly too, plausibly
  reflecting visibility and traffic-flow conditions rather than any
  single driver behavior.
- An unrecorded/unknown age band (plausibly a proxy for unlicensed or
  informally-recorded drivers) and day of week both rank in the top 12
  — worth investigating further, though I'd want more than a SHAP
  ranking alone before treating either as causal.

Mapping this back to Vietnam, the same categories of lever seem like
they'd matter there too: **junction design and signage at crossing-type
intersections**, **stricter enforcement around multi-vehicle collision
hotspots**, and **weather/visibility-aware traffic management**. I want
to be careful not to overclaim here — this is a correlational SHAP
ranking on Ethiopian data, not a Vietnamese study, and it can't prove
causation. What it does show is what a similar analysis on real
Vietnamese accident records — if that data ever became available —
would likely need to prioritize first.

## Discussion: what would a congestion-forecasting system need?

This project predicts accident **severity** — a genuinely different
problem from predicting traffic **congestion**, even though both fall
under "traffic management." I think it's worth being precise about the
difference, since it shapes what would actually help Vietnam next, and
because it would be easy to walk away from this project overclaiming
what a severity classifier can do.

**Different data entirely.** Severity classification needs individual
accident *records* — one row per crash. Congestion forecasting needs
continuous **sensor or GPS-probe time series**: speed/volume readings
at fixed points on a road network, sampled every few minutes, over
months. The standard public benchmarks — **METR-LA** (207 LA freeway
sensors) and **PEMS-BAY** (325 Bay Area sensors) — look nothing like
this project's data: no individual events, just continuous per-sensor
speed readings.

**Different modeling approach: spatio-temporal, not tabular.** This
project's classifiers treat every accident record as independent.
Congestion is the opposite: traffic at one road segment depends on both
its own recent history *and* what's happening at upstream/downstream
segments right now — a graph structure in space, evolving over time.
Standard approaches (**DCRNN**, **Graph WaveNet**) explicitly model the
road network as a graph, combining graph convolutions with recurrent/
temporal layers — not something a `RandomForestClassifier` or
`LGBMClassifier` (this project's tools) can express.

**What Vietnam specifically would need that this project's data can't
provide:**

- **A sensor network, or a substitute for one.** METR-LA/PEMS-BAY rely
  on fixed highway loop detectors — infrastructure Vietnam's urban roads
  mostly lack. The realistic substitute is crowd-sourced **GPS probe
  data** (ride-hailing/mapping apps) aggregated into road-segment speed
  estimates — a fundamentally different data-collection problem.
- **A model of mixed-vehicle flow.** Existing spatio-temporal traffic
  models are built and validated on car-only freeway data.
  Motorbike-dominated urban traffic (lane-splitting, informal lane use,
  far higher vehicle density per road width) behaves differently enough
  that the same architectures would need real validation on
  Vietnam-specific data before trusting them.
- **Integration with accident-risk findings like this project's own.**
  A genuinely useful combined system wouldn't just forecast where
  traffic will be slow — it would flag where slow-moving, high-density,
  mixed-vehicle conditions also historically correlate with severe
  accidents (this project's junction-type and multi-vehicle-collision
  findings above), turning two separate models into one early-warning
  system for both congestion *and* safety.

None of this is a limitation of this project — it's the honest scope
boundary between two real, different traffic-management problems, and
I'd rather name that boundary clearly than imply this one classifier
solves both.

## Conclusion

Working through a severely imbalanced, moderately messy, real accident
dataset — chosen for contextual relevance to a problem I couldn't get
open Vietnamese data for directly — taught me a few things I'd want to
carry into any future imbalanced-classification project: accuracy can
be actively misleading, class-weighting isn't automatically the right
fix (it just happened to win here, and only because I checked), and
correctly handling imbalance mattered more than model choice.

The biggest decision in this project turned out to be the target
itself, not the model. Measuring — rather than assuming — that the raw
3-class column left Fatal injury essentially undetected (~3% recall)
was the key step; collapsing Serious + Fatal into one **Severe** class
raised that to ~30-35% recall and macro-F1 from ~0.39 to ~0.60, a
substantial, measured improvement, not a marginal one. I think that's
the more general lesson: when a rare class isn't learnable, the fix
isn't always a fancier model or more resampling — sometimes it's asking
a different, still-useful question of the same data.

The SHAP explainability work pointed at concrete, actionable levers —
junction type, multi-vehicle collisions, time of day, and weather — that
I think would transfer conceptually to Vietnam's own traffic-safety
problem, even though this dataset can't prove that directly. Congestion
forecasting, the natural next traffic-management question, needs
different data and a different modeling paradigm entirely — a scope
boundary worth stating plainly rather than blurring.
